§7.3.7 QR Codes and Bar Codes

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

text-qr-codes-and-bar-codes · text images marks

✅ Normative

A QR code or bar code MUST be rendered as an image reference whose alt text holds the decoded content and whose target holds the literal label: ![decoded content](QR Code), ![decoded content](Bar code). The code MUST also be an element of its own, carrying the decoded value and a box around the code.

The rendering

![content of qr code](QR Code)
![content of Bar code](Bar code)

So a code that decodes to a tracking URL becomes ![https://example.com/t/9F2K](QR Code).

The alt-text and target slots are used in the reverse of the usual Markdown convention: the content goes in the alt slot, the literal label in the target slot. That is deliberate.

Why this form

It is the only encoding where the Markdown alone is useful. A reader gets the decoded payload — usually a URL or a tracking number — without following an element reference. The code's own element still carries the scan value, and its box locates the code for anyone who needs the image.

When the code does not decode

A payload MUST NOT be invented. A code that does not decode MUST be rendered with the label alone and an empty alt text, and is still its own element with its box:

![](QR Code)

Example

✅ Sample — a QR code closing a product page

A QR code printed at the foot of a product page, beside the line "Pour découvrir d'autres exemples, c'est ici :" — the prose leads directly into it, so dropping the code leaves a sentence pointing at nothing. The code on this page does not decode, so the alt text stays empty; had it decoded, its payload would fill the alt slot. The code is its own element, with a box around the code alone.

Expected Markdown · excerpt, foot of the block

…

Pour découvrir d'autres exemples, c'est ici :

![](QR Code)

Markdown source
<!-- … -->


Pour découvrir d'autres exemples, c'est ici :


![](QR Code)
